records.title: Kigali: water, mobility, waste and wetlands
records.answer: Kigali's service systems meet at the boundary between a growing city and the networks that supply it. Water expansion, transport investment, waste-treatment pilots and wetland restoration are progressing through different stages; a city-wide assessment needs to preserve those differences.
records.scope: One City of Kigali place account covering Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge districts. External water sources and regional transport connections remain dependencies, not extensions of the city boundary. Districts, treatment facilities and mobility schemes are not additional counted identities in this account.
records.stage: The November 2026 utility account retains water shortages and a 2027 expansion target. Other inspected records distinguish approved transport investment, inaugurated waste pilots and wetland restoration approaching completion. No blanket city-service readiness or comparable outcome-series admission is made.

identity_decision.rationale: Count the City of Kigali once as a municipal receiving-system account, with its three districts inside the named boundary. Karenge in Rwamagana and wider transport connections are external dependencies, not additional city territory. Nduba facilities, wetlands and RUMI are service examples rather than new project identities in this group. No prior counted place or historical acquisition docket is reused.

timeline.event: GGGI reported inauguration of Nduba's pilot waste facilities.
WASAC dates the start of the Karenge expansion to this month.
GGGI published the waste-study web summary; this is not its sampling date.
The World Bank announced RUMI financing approval.
WASAC reported Karenge construction progress and continuing service constraints.

sections.heading: One city and several service catchments
sections.text: Kigali's municipal overview defines a city of about 730 square kilometres comprising Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge. It assigns the city responsibilities for planning, infrastructure, transport, hygiene and water treatment, alongside coordination with other public bodies. These responsibilities provide a useful way to connect service decisions without assuming that one institution delivers everything. The administrative boundary is also narrower than some of the networks serving residents. A water source outside Kigali can be crucial to city supply without becoming city territory, while a transport terminal can serve regional passengers without making all their places of origin part of this account.

sections.heading: More water production must become dependable supply
sections.text: WASAC's November 13 account reports the Karenge expansion at 75 percent construction progress, with completion expected in 2027. The intended increase from 12,000 to 48,000 cubic metres per day combines a new treatment unit with rehabilitation and supporting intake, pipeline and reservoir work. Karenge is in Rwamagana, illustrating Kigali's dependence on infrastructure beyond its boundary. The same account identifies continuing shortages in areas including Ndera, Gasogi and Kanombe. More production capacity is therefore a delivery objective, not evidence that household taps already run continuously. The practical test extends through distribution: pressure, service hours, interruptions and the time or cost of obtaining water when piped service is unavailable.

sections.heading: Transport investment includes access and livelihoods
sections.text: The World Bank approved $100 million for RUMI in June 2025, supporting a Nyabugogo interchange, dedicated bus lanes, walking and cycling connections, electric buses and charging. Its expectation of up to 180,000 terminal passengers per day by 2030 is a forecast, not current patronage. Kigali's project page also identifies risks to nearby wetlands and potential economic displacement of small businesses around the bus park. Those issues belong beside the mobility benefits: improving a transfer can change who can trade, work or reach services nearby. The safeguard framework describes how impacts should be assessed and managed; it does not demonstrate completed compensation or restored livelihoods. Opening infrastructure and delivering affordable, accessible journeys remain different milestones.

sections.heading: Waste recovery depends on sorting and measurement
sections.text: GGGI's June 2024 inauguration account describes Nduba pilots for sorting, organic-waste treatment and weighing incoming trucks. The sorting facility is rated for 100 tons per day and the biowaste unit for five; those equipment ratings are not a city-wide diversion result. The later waste-study summary explains why measurement needs care. Samples came from direct household collections, redirected deliveries and commercial premises, and some materials had been exposed to rain. Added moisture increases measured mass, so as-received weights cannot be silently compared with dry-weight quantities. A credible recovery account needs both material flows and consistent weighing rules, including incoming waste, recovered products and residual disposal. The web summary's May 2025 publication date does not establish when the samples were collected.

sections.heading: Wetlands connect drainage with urban land use
sections.text: REMA describes restoration of five Kigali wetlands as approaching completion, with renewed vegetation, habitat and recreational space. It presents water storage and filtration as important functions alongside biodiversity. These connections matter because drainage, settlement and public space share the same landscape: the ecological role is not interchangeable with a landscaped park's visitor appeal. The undated account reports benefits but does not quantify protection during a particular storm or establish final acceptance of every site. Monitoring needs to follow storage, water quality and habitat through seasons, while keeping maintenance and surrounding land use visible. Restoration progress alone cannot supply a universal flood-protection guarantee.

sections.heading: Evidence test for everyday city services
sections.text: Editorial evidence test: start with a resident's service area and follow the responsible network across administrative boundaries. Compare water supply hours with accepted distribution works, actual journeys with terminal and street access, and waste recovery with compatible material accounting. Keep transport-related livelihood obligations visible rather than treating them as an appendix to construction. For wetlands, pair dated ecological and storm observations with maintenance responsibilities. Preserve reporting periods and distinguish design capacity from sustained service. A city assessment should show which combinations work, for whom and under what conditions, without borrowing an individual project's stage as a verdict on the whole place.
